newsitem.title: UK: Sterling down on the day after overnight surge.
newsitem.headline: Sterling down on the day after overnight surge.

text.p: Sterling surged overnight to its best level since crashing out of the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992, but if it climbs much higher there could be squeals from the authorities, analysts said on Tuesday.
Reams of data pointing to a buoyant British economy, driven by rampant consumer demand, have stoked speculation of interest rate rises and sent yield-hungry investors into pounds.

But with consumers spending fairly freely, monetary easing is out of the question -- leaving the economy's managers few weapons with which to restrain a strong currency. "It's got to the level now at which the authorities might be getting slightly concerned, in terms of how much stronger can the currency be allowed to get," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

British companies have already expressed anxiety over a rally which has sent sterling to four-year highs against both the mark and the dollar, damaging British competitiveness by making exports more expensive and cheapening imports.
Sterling hit a peak of 2.6370 marks overnight before profit taking pulled it back to around 2.61 at European midsession.
"If it was to push towards 2.65/2.70 you might start to get comments from the authorities trying to reverse it," Barr said.

The markets are currently hypersensitive to comments from officials, analysts noted. The dollar's sharp overnight rise -- which helped catapult sterling upwards against the mark -- was sparked by a remark from Bundesbank council member Otmar Issing.
Issing told a bankers' forum that uncertainty about the stability of the European single currency might prompt a shift out of marks into dollar-denominated investments.

The dollar's rally was stoked by New York Federal Reserve Bank president William McDonough, who said the U.S. unit might become more important as a reserve currency in the run-up to European monetary union.
But verbal intervention has its limits.

"Talking is difficult -- if you start to talk, the market expects a policy to reflect it. If they're not prepared to back it up with policy action, what can they do?" asked Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank here.

Figures showing U.K. official reserves fell $98 million in November, after rising $7.0 million in October, suggest the Bank of England did not try to dampen sterling last month by selling it for other currencies, analysts said.

"It does not suggest that the Bank of England has expressed any concern at the rise in the pound -- at least it has not put its money where its thoughts are," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at BankAmerica here.
A U.K. Treasury official said on Tuesday that sterling's rally would have a downward effect on retail prices.
But though currency strength might have a short-term anti-inflationary effect, analysts said the Bank of England will not be convinced of the longer-term impact on inflation.
And while Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has so far stayed silent, he will not welcome industry complaints in the run-up to the general election, which must be held by May.
Actions may speak louder than words, but words may be all the authorities have in the current situation, analysts said.
"A sterling rally does take off some of the pressure to raise rates," said Deutsche's Barr. "But if you were to cut rates that would just add fuel to an already overstoked fire."
